On the way home to Kishkindha, the triumphant search party comes to the Madhuvana, the honey forest: King Sugriva's private, carefully guarded orchard. And they are very, very hungry. Big wins can come with a celebration that gets a little out of hand, and the Sundara Kanda has one too. It's wonderfully undignified.

segments.voice: First, a serious moment. After Hanuman's report, Angada has a bold idea: why not go back to Lanka ourselves, defeat Ravana, and bring Sita to Rama? Jambavan, the old bear, says no. Our task was to find her and to tell Rama. The rescue is Rama's to make, as Sita herself said in the grove: let Rama come. So they set off north. Then the Madhuvana. With Angada's permission, the monkeys fall on the honey. They eat it, drink it, dance, sing, wrestle, tumble out of the trees, stagger about, and Valmiki tells it with obvious enjoyment. The orchard's guardian is Dadhimukha, Sugriva's uncle, and when he tries to stop them, they shove him around. Furious, he rushes to King Sugriva. Your honey forest is ruined; Angada's band has torn it to pieces. And Sugriva's reaction is the best part. He's not angry. He's thrilled. He turns to Rama and Lakshmana and says, in effect: they would never dare do this unless they'd succeeded. They've found Sita. A wrecked orchard becomes good news for Rama, at last. Sugriva reads the mess the way Jambavan read the roar on the shore. Dadhimukha is sent back to tell the monkeys to come at once. And Hanuman is about to stand in front of Rama.

632.title: "seen, Sita"
632.hook: Hanuman has the biggest news of Rama's life, and he chooses his first word with care
632.carry: he arranges his words around Rama's fear
632.howItsDone: Ramayana teachers, in temples and in family readings, often pause on Hanuman's first word, seen, as a lesson in how to speak; Kamban's Tamil Ramayana gives the same moment as I saw.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the return. The search party wrecked Sugriva's honey forest, and your line, a wrecked orchard, good news, is how Sugriva read it.
screen: `THE RETURN: A WRECKED ORCHARD, GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Rama has been waiting on a mountain outside Kishkindha. The search parties from the north, the east and the west have already come back with nothing. Now the southern party arrives, loud and happy, and Hanuman steps forward. He has crossed the sea, found her, spoken with her, fought half of Lanka and left it burning. He has a long, astonishing story to tell. And first he has to decide which word comes out of his mouth.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, AND NO NEWS.` → `THREE PARTIES CAME BACK EMPTY.` → `WHICH WORD FIRST?`

segments.voice: The word he puts first, in Valmiki's Sanskrit, is drishta. Seen. He bows and tells Rama the queen has been seen, that she is keeping her vows, that she is unharmed. Think about the order. If he had begun with the ocean, or Lanka, or the words I went, Rama would have spent every sentence waiting, heart in his throat. If he had begun with her name alone, Rama might have braced for the worst. Seen comes first, and the fear is answered before it can rise. The Tamil poet Kamban, retelling the story, makes it even sharper: his Hanuman opens with the Tamil for I saw, before he names her at all. Only then does Hanuman tell the rest: the leap, the city at night, the ashoka grove, a thin woman under a tree, Ravana's threats, Rama's own ring passed down through the branches. Joy comes over Rama and Lakshmana as they listen. Sugriva had already guessed, from the monkeys' wild celebration on the way home. It's one word in a very long epic, but it shows who Hanuman is. He can leap an ocean. Here his greatness is quieter: before he speaks, he thinks about where his words will land. He arranges his sentence around someone else's fear.

633.title: "seen, Sita"
633.hook: a hair jewel, a story only Rama would know, and a month on the clock: the beautiful book comes to rest
633.howItsDone: Hindu families and temples recite the Sundara Kanda on its own as a complete reading, often over several days and especially in difficult times, and it closes with Rama holding Sita's jewel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman put seen first, so Rama's fear was answered before the story began. Your line: he arranges his words around Rama's fear.

Hanuman has told the story. Now he opens his hand. In it is a jewel Sita wore in her hair; in the ashoka grove she untied it and gave it to him, so that Rama would believe every word. Rama takes it, holds it against his chest, and weeps. Lakshmana stands beside him. To anyone else it's an ornament. To the two men looking at it, it's her.
screen: `HANUMAN OPENS HIS HAND.` → `A JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` → `RAMA WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Rama knows the jewel at once. In Valmiki he says it came to Sita from her father, King Janaka, at their wedding, and that seeing it is almost like seeing her. Then he asks Hanuman again and again: what did she say? Tell me her exact words. So Hanuman passes on everything. Sita had sent a second token, and it was a story: the crow at Chitrakuta that kept attacking her, and the single blade of grass Rama sent after it as a weapon. Nobody else was there. A memory used as a password. And she sent a message with a deadline: she could hold on for one more month, and no longer. So the joy of seen arrives with a clock attached, and Rama's grief and resolve rise together. Why is this book called Sundara, beautiful? People give different answers, and nobody can say for certain which one Valmiki meant. But Hindu tradition treats the Sundara Kanda as a book of hope. It's recited on its own, start to finish, at home or in a temple, especially in hard times, because it's the stretch of the story where the lost is found and the long wait finally hears seen. And notice where the beautiful book comes to rest. Not on the leap, not on the burning city. On a man holding a hair ornament and asking to hear her words one more time.

634.title: the bridge
634.hook: the war book opens with an embrace, a march, and a sea nobody can cross
634.howItsDone: The Yuddha Kanda is the longest book of Valmiki's Ramayana; Hindu storytellers and reciters often open it with Rama's embrace of Hanuman, a moment many devotees of Hanuman treasure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line, tell me her words again: a jewel, a crow story only Rama would know, and the Sundara Kanda closed. Today the sixth book begins: the Yuddha Kanda, the war book.

The war book doesn't open with a war. It opens with a thank-you. Rama turns to Hanuman and tries to say what he's done: crossed an ocean, found her, come back. Then Rama looks at himself: an exile in bark clothes, living on a mountain, with no kingdom, no treasury, no land to give. So he says the one gift he has left is this, and he takes Hanuman in his arms.
screen: `NOT A WAR. A THANK-YOU.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO GIVE.` → `AN EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Then the thank-you turns into a question. Hanuman crossed the ocean alone, by leaping. An army can't leap. Rama says it plainly: how will all of us get across? Sugriva answers like a good friend in a crisis. Grief makes a person slow, he says. Let's move, and find the way when we're there. So the army marches south, and Valmiki makes it huge and noisy: monkey and bear troops spreading over hills and forests, Sugriva and Lakshmana beside Rama, Hanuman carrying him on his shoulders at times. They reach the southern shore and make camp at the edge of the land. And there it is: the ocean, roaring, full of sea creatures, rising and falling as if it were breathing, with no far shore in sight. That night Rama can't rest. He stands at the water's edge and speaks to the wind. You blow where she is. Touch her, and then come and touch me. The general who has to cross the sea is also a husband on a beach in the dark. Hold onto this picture: the army behind him, the water in front, and no way over. Everything in the next few days answers it. A bridge doesn't begin with stones. It begins with someone at the edge, admitting there's no way across yet.

635.title: the bridge
635.hook: three nights of asking, one burst of anger, and the ocean finally speaks
635.howItsDone: Rama's vigil and the ocean's answer are told in recitations of the Yuddha Kanda; at Rameswaram, the coastal town tradition links with this story, pilgrims bathe in the sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, before a single stone. Rama on the shore at night, asking the wind to touch her, and your line, an army on a beach.

Rama spreads kusha grass on the sand, the sharp ritual grass, and lies down on it, facing the sea. He folds his hands, asking the god of the ocean, Sagara, to show him a way across. One night passes. Nothing. Two nights. Three nights, fasting, waiting, and the water just keeps coming in and going out as if no one were there.
screen: `A BED OF KUSHA GRASS.` → `THREE NIGHTS OF ASKING.` → `NO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: On the fourth morning Rama gets up angry. Gentleness, he tells Lakshmana, is taken for weakness. He takes up his bow and starts firing into the sea. The waves heave, the sea creatures thrash, the water churns as if the end of the world had come. Lakshmana catches his brother's arm: enough. And Rama fits a terrible weapon to the bow, ready to dry the ocean to its floor. That's when the ocean rises. Sagara comes up out of the water in person, shining, garlanded, with the rivers around him, and speaks with folded hands. I can't change what I am. Earth, wind, sky, water, fire: each keeps its own nature, and mine is to be deep and hard to cross. I won't dry up, and I won't go still. But if you build, I'll hold it up. And you already have the builder: Nala, son of Vishvakarma, the craftsman of the gods. One problem remains. The arrow on Rama's bow can't simply be put down. So, at the ocean's suggestion, Rama sends it north, to a place of wrongdoers, and Valmiki says the land it struck became a desert. Look at the shape of this. The answer was never to make the sea stop being the sea. The bridge isn't built against the ocean. It's built with the ocean's help.

636.title: the bridge
636.hook: five days, a whole army of builders, and the stories people added later
636.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Rameswaram and Dhanushkodi on India's southeastern coast, linked by tradition to the bridge, and the squirrel's story is a common children's tale.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, promised. The ocean said it couldn't change what it was, but gave your line, I'll hold it up, and named Nala as the builder.

Nala steps forward, and what he says is quietly funny. The ocean is right. I'm Vishvakarma's son, and I have my father's skill. I can build this. Then he adds, more or less: nobody asked me, so I didn't mention it. An army has been staring at an impossible sea, and the one person who could solve it was standing in the crowd, waiting to be asked. Then the work begins.
screen: `NALA STEPS FORWARD.` → `NOBODY ASKED ME.` → `THE WORK BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki loves the noise of it. The monkeys and bears pour into the forests and tear up trees by the thousand: palms, ashokas, flowering trees of every kind. They drag boulders down from the hills and heave them into the water with a sound like thunder. Some hold measuring lines while others lay the stones. And he counts the days. Fourteen yojanas the first day, twenty the second, then twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three. In five days it's done: a bridge a hundred yojanas long and ten wide, straight across the sea. The gods watch from the sky, amazed, and the army crosses to the shore of Lanka. Two things you may have heard aren't in Valmiki. One is the squirrel, who rolls in the sand and shakes it onto the bridge, and Rama strokes its back, and the stripes are his fingers. The other is the stones that float because Rama's name is written on them. Both come from later retellings and oral tradition, and devotees tell them as lessons in devotion: no gift is too small, and the name carries weight. It's worth knowing which is which. Today the line of shoals between Rameswaram in India and Mannar in Sri Lanka is called Rama Setu, Rama's bridge, in Hindu tradition. People hold different views about what that chain of shoals is, and those arguments go on. What Valmiki gives is simpler: a whole people, five days, one bridge.

637.title: Vibhishana's crossing
637.hook: Ravana's own brother tells him the truth in council, and pays for it
637.howItsDone: Hindu tellers honor Vibhishana as a model of righteousness and surrender, and often dwell on his advice in Ravana's council and on his words about rare, honest counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, built in five days under Nala, and your line, a whole people, one bridge.

Go back to Lanka, just after Hanuman left it burning. Ravana calls his council. A monkey has walked into his city, killed his soldiers and set his houses on fire, and an army is gathering across the sea. The ministers stand up one by one, and every one says the same thing. You've beaten the gods, king. Who is this Rama? We'll crush him. It's the sound of a room where everyone has learned what the boss likes to hear. Then one person stands up and says something else.
screen: `RAVANA'S COUNCIL.` → `EVERYONE SAYS THE SAME THING.` → `ONE VOICE SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: It's Vibhishana, Ravana's younger brother. Valmiki places this before the bridge is built; we told the bridge first, and now we step back. Vibhishana speaks carefully, like someone who loves the person he's about to anger. Give Sita back. Taking another man's wife was wrong, and it will destroy you, and all of us with you. Rama has done you no harm. Return her, and Lanka lives. Ravana won't hear it. In Valmiki his answer is cruel: better to live with an enemy, or a cobra, than with a kinsman who secretly works for your enemy. He calls his brother a disgrace to the family, and says anyone else who spoke like this would be dead already. So Vibhishana rises into the air with four companions and speaks from above the hall. You're my elder brother, and I owe you respect. I said this for your good. People who say pleasant things are easy to find. People who say hard, useful things, and people willing to hear them, are rare. Then he leaves. He crosses the sea, stops in the sky above Rama's camp, and calls down: I am Ravana's brother, Vibhishana. I've left everything behind. I've come to Rama for refuge. And so the week closes: from the return, to seen, Sita, to a bridge in five days, to a brother hanging in the air over an enemy camp, asking to be let in.
screen: `GIVE SITA BACK.` · `A KINSMAN WORSE THAN A COBRA.` · `I SAID IT FOR YOUR GOOD.` · `I'VE COME FOR REFUGE.` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM SEEN TO SANCTUARY.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone told you something hard that turned out to be true, and how you took it at first; then think of something hard you may need to say to someone you love. Don't rehearse it, just notice where the care is in it and where the fear is, and breathe with both, side by side.
